title: Attackers, defenders and blockers: the playing styles
seo_title: Table tennis playing styles: attackers, defenders, blockers
description: The table tennis playing styles explained: attackers, all-rounders, blockers and choppers, where each stands, what spin they use and how to pick your own.
summary: Most top players attack with topspin, but choppers, blockers and pimples players win matches too. Here is how each style works, who plays it and how to find yours.
key_points: Attackers try to win the point with topspin, mostly the heavy topspin stroke called the loop; most top players attack.
All-rounders attack first but are just as comfortable blocking and counter-attacking.
Blockers stand close to the table and use the opponent's pace against them.
Choppers defend from well back with backspin and are now rare at the top, though Hitomi Sato is in the women's top 10.
Learn to attack first; a style grows out of your strengths, your grip and your rubbers.
body: A playing style is your usual way of winning points: where you stand, which spin you use and whether you try to finish the rally or make your opponent miss. The main styles are attackers, who win points with topspin; all-rounders, who mix attack and defence; blockers, who stay close to the table and absorb the opponent's power; and defenders or choppers, who stand back and return the ball with backspin. Most top players are attackers, but every style still wins matches at club level and beyond.

Styles overlap, and the labels are loose. The American coach Larry Hodges, writing for Butterfly, says "there are as many playing styles as there are players in the world". Think of the categories below as starting points.

Attackers aim to make the ball dip on to the table fast and spinning, mainly with the loop, a stroke that brushes up the back of the ball for heavy topspin. A two-winged looper attacks from both forehand and backhand; others build their game round a big forehand. Some attackers play close to the table and take the ball early; others step back and exchange loops from mid-distance.

This is the dominant style in the professional game. Nine of the top 10 women in the world rankings of November 2026, and all of the top 10 men, are attackers or attacking all-rounders. Our guide to [spin](/guide/spin-in-table-tennis-explained.html) explains why topspin is so effective.

All-rounders can attack and defend equally well and choose according to the ball. Hodges says the best players "are mostly better on the attack" but "are all comfortable whether attacking or reacting to the opponent's attack", which for him means blocking and counter-attacking as well as looping. Sweden's Truls Moregard, the world No 6, is a creative example: a shakehand player known for backhand blocks and punches and for unorthodox shots.

Blockers stand close to the table and use short, firm strokes to send the opponent's attack straight back, often to a different corner. Butterfly's coach Han Xiao calls the blocker "one of the most common defensive archetypes", whose aim is "to use close to the table blocking to negate the opponent's attacks". A common hybrid blocks with the backhand and waits for a ball to attack with the forehand.

Many blockers use pimpled rubber on one side. Short pimples are less affected by the opponent's spin; long pimples return the ball with spin that is hard to read. Our guide to [rubbers](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) explains how each works.

Choppers, in Han Xiao's words, "defend from mid-distance as well as far from the table, using primarily backspin strokes". The chop is a downward stroke that sends the ball back low with backspin, and good choppers vary the amount so the attacker never quite knows how much is on it. Many play with inverted rubber on the forehand and long pimples on the backhand, and turn the bat to swap sides during a rally.

Pure defenders are rare at the top. Han Xiao wrote in 2015 that "there are very few pure defensive players remaining at the professional level". Those who succeed today are mostly modern defenders, who chop but counter-attack whenever the ball sits up. Japan's Hitomi Sato, world No 9 in November 2026, and Germany's Han Ying, an Olympic team silver medallist in 2016, are two of the best. The Chop, Eleven's site for [defensive table tennis](/defensive/), follows every leading defender.

Rallies between two choppers can last a long time, which is why the rules include the expedite rule. If a game lasts 10 minutes, unless at least 18 points have been scored, or if both players ask for it earlier, the players serve one point each in turn and the receiver wins the point by making 13 good returns in a rally. Once it starts, it stays in force for the rest of the match. Our [rules explained](/guide/table-tennis-rules-explained.html) guide has the detail.

A rarer defensive style is lobbing, or fishing: standing far back and returning smashes with high, spinning balls until the attacker misses. Han Xiao names Japan's Jun Mizutani as a fine exponent. Most players use it only as an emergency shot, but in the right hands it can turn a rally round.

Start by learning to attack. Every style depends on solid topspin strokes, and even choppers need to counter-attack to win at a good level. Your style will grow from your strengths: how quickly you move, whether you prefer to take the ball early or late, and what your [grip](/guide/penhold-vs-shakehand-grip.html) suits. After a season or two, a coach at your club can help you decide whether a defensive style or pimpled rubber fits your game.

Then learn to play against the others. Hodges's advice is to learn to "adjust to any style": against a chopper, for instance, he notes that most are weak "in the middle, around their elbow area". The serve and the return of serve shape every one of these styles, which is the subject of our guide to [serve and receive tactics](/guide/serve-and-receive-tactics.html).
